title: Final Case Study: The Campus Merch Shop
explanation: You've been hired as the data analyst for a small campus merch shop. There are three tables: customers (who shops), products (what's for sale), and orders (who bought what, and how many). Each order row links a customer_id to a product_id. No new commands in this lesson — your job is to combine everything you've learned to answer real business questions. Read each question slowly, decide which tables you need, then build your query one piece at a time.

example.code:
SELECT c.name, SUM(o.quantity * p.price) AS spent
FROM orders o
JOIN customers c ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id
JOIN products p ON o.product_id = p.product_id
GROUP BY c.name
ORDER BY spent DESC;

lines.line: SELECT c.name, SUM(o.quantity * p.price) AS spent
lines.explain: Show each customer's name and the total money they spent (quantity times price, added up).
Start from the orders table and call it o for short.

lines.line: JOIN customers c ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id
lines.explain: Bring in the customer's name by matching customer IDs.

lines.line: JOIN products p ON o.product_id = p.product_id
lines.explain: Bring in each product's price by matching product IDs.
Make one group per customer so SUM adds up their orders.
Put the biggest spender at the top.

tasks.prompt: The owner wants to know how many items were sold in each product category. Show category and total quantity sold (call it items_sold), biggest first.
tasks.answer: SELECT p.category, SUM(o.quantity) AS items_sold FROM orders o JOIN products p ON o.product_id = p.product_id GROUP BY p.category ORDER BY items_sold DESC;
hints: You need orders (for quantity) and products (for category). Join them on product_id.
GROUP BY p.category, then SUM(o.quantity). Finish with ORDER BY items_sold DESC.

solution_lines.explain: Show each category and how many items it sold.

solution_lines.line: FROM orders o JOIN products p ON o.product_id = p.product_id
solution_lines.explain: Link each order to its product.

tasks.prompt: Which products have never been ordered? Show just their names.
tasks.answer: SELECT p.name FROM products p LEFT JOIN orders o ON p.product_id = o.product_id WHERE o.order_id IS NULL;
hints: Start from products and LEFT JOIN orders, so products with no orders still show up.
Products with no match have NULL in the orders columns — filter with WHERE o.order_id IS NULL.

solution_lines.line: FROM products p LEFT JOIN orders o ON p.product_id = o.product_id
solution_lines.explain: Keep every product, even ones with no orders.
Keep only products that never matched an order.

tasks.prompt: Show each city and its total revenue (quantity times price, call it revenue). Only show cities with more than $100 in revenue.
tasks.answer: SELECT c.city, SUM(o.quantity * p.price) AS revenue FROM orders o JOIN customers c ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id JOIN products p ON o.product_id = p.product_id GROUP BY c.city HAVING SUM(o.quantity * p.price) > 100;
hints: You need all three tables: orders, customers (for city), and products (for price).
GROUP BY c.city, then use HAVING (not WHERE) to keep only revenue over 100.

solution_lines.line: SELECT c.city, SUM(o.quantity * p.price) AS revenue
solution_lines.explain: Show each city and the money it brought in.

solution_lines.line: JOIN customers c ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id
JOIN products p ON o.product_id = p.product_id

solution_lines.explain: Keep only cities over $100 — HAVING filters groups.

tasks.prompt: Predict: how many rows will this query return?
hints: DISTINCT removes repeats. Count how many different customers placed orders.
Look at customer_id in orders: 1 to 6 show up. Customers 7 and 8 never ordered.

solution_lines.explain: Lists each customer who ordered, once each — 6 people.

tasks.prompt: Final challenge: label each customer as a 'Big Spender' (spent $80 or more) or 'Regular' (less). Use a WITH block to work out each customer's total first, then show name, spent, and the label (call it tier). Biggest spender first.
tasks.answer: WITH totals AS (SELECT o.customer_id, SUM(o.quantity * p.price) AS spent FROM orders o JOIN products p ON o.product_id = p.product_id GROUP BY o.customer_id) SELECT c.name, t.spent, CASE WHEN t.spent >= 80 THEN 'Big Spender' ELSE 'Regular' END AS tier FROM totals t JOIN customers c ON t.customer_id = c.customer_id ORDER BY t.spent DESC;
hints: Step 1: in a WITH block called totals, join orders and products and SUM(quantity * price) per customer_id.
Step 2: join totals to customers for the name, and use CASE WHEN spent >= 80 THEN 'Big Spender' ELSE 'Regular' END AS tier.

solution_lines.explain: Make a temporary table called totals.

solution_lines.line: SELECT o.customer_id, SUM(o.quantity * p.price) AS spent
solution_lines.explain: Work out how much each customer spent.

solution_lines.line: FROM orders o JOIN products p ON o.product_id = p.product_id
CASE WHEN t.spent >= 80 THEN 'Big Spender' ELSE 'Regular' END AS tier
solution_lines.explain: Label each customer by how much they spent.

solution_lines.line: FROM totals t JOIN customers c ON t.customer_id = c.customer_id

recap: You just did a real analyst's job: joining three tables, grouping, filtering groups with HAVING, finding missing data with LEFT JOIN, and building a step-by-step answer with WITH and CASE. That's the core of everyday SQL — congratulations on finishing the course!
